claims.claim: Aggregate representation reduction of 84.5%, clearing the 80% gate
claims.evidence: Reproduced to every digit at 84.5%. 3 of 3 alternative aggregates fall below the gate: equal weight 74.3%, lossless only 77.0%, without the anti-pattern baseline 55.6%.

claims.claim: Sharing a system prompt across sessions uses less memory
claims.evidence: At 1,024 sessions the live heap falls 32.8% against the JSON prediction of 49.5%. A plain object reference reaches 32.9% with no engine.

claims.claim: A rhyme stores about 29% less when sessions share a shape and differ in words
claims.evidence: True of JSON bytes (29.0%). In the live heap at 1,024 sessions the shipped engine saves 10.3%, and a tighter encoding of the same idea 30.4%, against 24.1% for a plain reference.

claims.claim: An exact-text cache wins when every session repeats the same words
claims.evidence: Reproduced: cache 164 bytes, rhyme 4,691 bytes. The cache is first smaller at 40% duplicates on the tested grid.

claims.claim: Lower latency from reconstructing a working set
claims.evidence: In process, materializing a session takes 1.81× and 11.44× the duplicated store's time for the two workloads, or 1.04× and 1.24× without cloning.

Direction reproduced on this host: 1.38× to 3.43× per turn. Decode alone 0.99× to 1.02×; prefill plus decode 1.07× to 1.56×. The tested mechanism is prefix reuse, which a prefix cache already provides. Logits match a full prefill to within 1.4e-4 on distilgpt2, where the check catches a cache built from the wrong prefix. On tiny-gpt2 it does not, so those turns show nothing.
Warmed up and with arms interleaved, this host gives 0.98× to 1.02×. Both arms perform the same steps per round; the original lab ran one arm first with no warm-up.

claims.claim: GPU allocation falls 81.4%, from 288.00 to 53.60 MiB
claims.evidence: Reproduced to every digit by arithmetic, with no GPU, because the value follows from requested buffer sizes and an assumed 15% delta. It is not a device reading, and no experiment here measures that assumption.

claims.claim: nvidia-smi peak falls 72.8%, from 313 to 85 MiB (historical, GTX 860M)
claims.evidence: Needs NVIDIA hardware; the lab reports not_run on this host (nvcuda_unavailable). A real-model analogue is measured here: key-value residency 84.4% on the MPS allocator, 27.3% once weights are counted.
Needs NVIDIA hardware. The copied payload alone is 9.41× smaller than the conventional one, so the byte count predicts most of the speedups recorded in the two stored receipts (9.60× and 11.24×).

claims.claim: A DRAM or accelerator memory reduction of 80% for AI serving
claims.evidence: Not established by any receipt. Key-value residency alone can exceed that (84.4% here), but counting weights gives 27.3% here and 50.8% on the H100 roofline, and a prefix cache gets the same residency.

claims.claim: `tiny benchmark` produces receipts on your machine
claims.evidence: False before this work: on a host with no GPU it reported a stored laptop receipt as a fresh pass, naming that laptop as the device. Labs now report only what ran in the current invocation, and a regression test pins it. On this host the GPU lab's status is not_run and the suite's verdict is incomplete.

E.note: The working set is the closure of one request. Vectors outside it are not represented, so it cannot reconstruct the lattice.

device.name: NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB
device.source: NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s

h100.honesty: Simulation on a published H100 SXM profile. Peak-bandwidth copy time is an upper bound, not a predicted wall clock. Tiny Footprint is given the same resident KV as a production prefix cache, because this lab has not measured a KV compression factor. The in-process 84.5% representation cut is not applied to device memory.
